title: REG U2·W1 — C Corporation Taxation (CPA Core)
lessonHtml:
Cold open — a separate taxpayer, taxed twice

Unit 1 taxed the individual owner directly. A C corporation is different: it is its own taxpayer, so its profits are taxed once at the entity level and again when distributed as dividends — the classic double taxation. If Jordan Reed incorporated MBG as a C corporation, the construction profit would face the 21% corporate tax and then a second tax on any dividend to Reed. This week covers formation, the corporate income computation, distributions, and liquidation.

Formation under §351

§351 makes incorporation tax-free when property is transferred solely in exchange for stock and the transferors, as a group, control the corporation — owning at least 80% of the voting power and shares — immediately after the exchange. Services do not count as property (stock for services is compensation income). If the transferor also receives boot (cash or other property), gain is recognized up to the lesser of the boot or the realized gain. Worked example: Reed contributes equipment with a $40,000 basis and $100,000 FMV solely for 100% of the new corporation's stock — no gain is recognized, Reed's stock basis is $40,000 (carryover), and the corporation takes the equipment at a $40,000 transferred basis. With $10,000 of cash boot, Reed would recognize $10,000 of gain (lesser of $10,000 boot or $60,000 realized).

Computing corporate taxable income

A C corporation's taxable income is gross income minus deductions, taxed at a flat 21% rate. Most ordinary and necessary business expenses are deductible, but several items follow special corporate rules. Unlike an individual, a corporation has no standard deduction, no QBI deduction, and no preferential capital-gains rate — net capital gains are taxed at the ordinary 21%.

Special corporate deductions

Three recur on the exam. The charitable contribution deduction is, under Public Law 119-21 §70426 (effective 2026), allowed only for contributions exceeding a 1%-of-taxable-income floor and is capped at 10% of taxable income (computed before the charitable, DRD, and a few other deductions); amounts above the 10% ceiling carry forward five years, while the portion below the 1% floor is disallowed under the new floor rule and is accounted for separately from the 10%-ceiling carryforward. Organizational and start-up expenditures may be partially expensed with the remainder amortized over 180 months. The dividends-received deduction (DRD) mitigates triple taxation of inter-corporate dividends: a corporation deducts 50% of dividends from a payer it owns less than 20% of, 65% if it owns 20% to 80%, and 100% if it owns 80% or more — subject to a taxable-income limitation that does not apply when the full DRD creates or increases an NOL.

Capital losses and net operating losses

Corporate loss rules differ sharply from the individual rules. A corporation's net capital loss offsets only capital gains — never ordinary income — and is carried back 3 years and forward 5 as a short-term loss. A corporate net operating loss arising after 2017 has no carryback, is carried forward indefinitely, and offsets only 80% of taxable income in a future year. These rules, with the special deductions above, drive the M-1 reconciliation below.

Book-tax differences (Schedules M-1 and M-3)

Because financial (book) income and taxable income diverge, a corporation reconciles them on Schedule M-1 (or the detailed M-3 for larger entities). Permanent differences (tax-exempt municipal interest, the 50% meals limit, federal income tax expense, fines) never reverse; temporary differences (depreciation, warranty accruals, deferred compensation) reverse over time and create the deferred taxes from FAR Unit 2. The M-1 starts with book net income and adds back nondeductible items and subtracts nontaxable income to arrive at taxable income.

Distributions and earnings and profits

A distribution to shareholders is a taxable dividend to the extent of the corporation's earnings and profits (E&P) — a tax concept similar to but distinct from retained earnings. Beyond E&P, the distribution is a return of capital that reduces the shareholder's stock basis, and any excess is capital gain. A corporation that distributes appreciated property recognizes gain as if it sold the property at FMV (but not loss). This ordering — dividend, then basis recovery, then gain — is a reliable exam pattern.

Liquidations, penalty taxes, and the corporate AMT

In a complete liquidation under §331, the shareholder treats the distribution as a sale of the stock, recognizing capital gain or loss, and the corporation generally recognizes gain or loss on the distributed property. A §332 liquidation of an 80%-owned subsidiary into its parent is tax-free to both. Two penalty taxes discourage hoarding earnings to defer the shareholder-level tax: the accumulated earnings tax (on earnings retained beyond reasonable business needs) and the personal holding company tax (on closely held corporations with mostly passive income). Finally, a 15% corporate alternative minimum tax applies to the financial-statement income of very large corporations (those averaging over $1 billion of book income) — not to a contractor the size of MBG, but testable.

Consolidated returns, reorganizations, and small-business stock

Related corporations get special regimes. An affiliated group connected through 80% ownership may elect to file a consolidated return, combining members' incomes and deferring gains on intercompany transactions until the asset leaves the group. Tax-free reorganizations let corporations combine without immediate tax when the deal has a business purpose and continuity of interest: a Type A statutory merger, a Type B stock-for-stock acquisition (solely for voting stock, ending in 80% control), and a Type C stock-for-substantially-all-assets acquisition are the most tested; boot triggers gain and the acquirer takes a carryover basis. Worked DRD: if MBG Corp owns 30% of a supplier and receives a $100,000 dividend, the 65% DRD is $65,000, leaving $35,000 taxed at 21% (absent the taxable-income limitation).

Two shareholder-favorable provisions round out the basics. §1244 stock lets an individual treat a loss on qualifying small-business-corporation stock as an ordinary loss (up to $50,000, or $100,000 MFJ) instead of capital — a rare conversion in the taxpayer's favor. §1202 excludes gain on qualified small business stock; for stock acquired after the July 4, 2025 enactment of Public Law 119-21 §70431 the exclusion is tiered — 50% after a 3-year hold, 75% after 4 years, and 100% after 5 years — with an expanded per-issuer limitation (stock acquired earlier keeps the prior more-than-five-years rule). Both reward investing in small C corporations and are frequent distractors against the general capital-gain rules.

CMA bridge

FAR Unit 2 measured the deferred taxes that temporary book-tax differences create; REG shows the return side — the M-1 reconciliation, the 21% rate, the DRD, and the E&P that determines whether a distribution to MBG's owner is a dividend, a return of capital, or a capital gain. The entity choice itself (C corp double tax vs passthrough) is next week's decision.

Practice and recap

  1. Apply §351: tax-free if property is exchanged for stock and transferors control ≥80%; boot triggers gain up to the lesser of boot or realized gain.
  2. Tax corporate income at a flat 21%; apply the DRD (50/65/100%) and the 10%-of-taxable-income charitable limit.
  3. Remember corporate capital losses offset only capital gains (back 3/forward 5) and post-2017 NOLs carry forward indefinitely at an 80% limit.
  4. Order distributions: dividend to the extent of E&P, then return of capital, then capital gain.

Recap: a C corporation is a separate 21% taxpayer with double taxation; §351 defers gain on a controlled-corporation formation (Reed's $40,000-basis equipment for 100% stock = no gain, $40,000 carryover bases); the DRD is 50/65/100% by ownership; corporate capital losses offset only capital gains; and a distribution is a dividend only to the extent of E&P, then a return of capital and finally capital gain — while §1244 can turn a small-corporation stock loss ordinary.

flashcards.back: No gain/loss when property is transferred solely for stock and transferors control ≥80% immediately after; boot triggers gain up to the lesser of boot or realized gain.

questions.q: Under §351, incorporation is tax-free if transferors of property receive stock and, immediately after, control the corporation by owning at least:
questions.explain: §351 requires the transferor group to control at least 80% of voting power and shares immediately after the exchange.

questions.q: The C corporation income tax rate is a flat:
questions.explain: C corporations are taxed at a flat 21% rate.

questions.q: The dividends-received deduction for a corporation owning 20% to 80% of the payer is:
A C corporation's net capital loss may be:
choices: Carried back 3 years and forward 5, offsetting only capital gains
Deducted up to $3,000 against ordinary income
Carried forward indefinitely against ordinary income
questions.explain: Corporate capital losses offset only capital gains and carry back 3/forward 5 years.

questions.q: A corporate distribution is a taxable dividend to the extent of the corporation's:
questions.explain: Distributions are dividends to the extent of E&P; beyond E&P they reduce basis, then create capital gain.

questions.q: Reed contributes equipment (basis $40,000, FMV $100,000) solely for 100% of a new corporation's stock. Reed's recognized gain and stock basis are:
questions.explain: §351 defers the gain; the stock takes a $40,000 carryover (substituted) basis.

questions.q: A C corporation NOL arising in 2026 is:
choices: Carried forward indefinitely and limited to 80% of taxable income
questions.explain: Post-2017 NOLs have no carryback, carry forward indefinitely, and are limited to 80% of taxable income.
